title: Principles of chemical thermodynamics and kinetics

A) HIGH-YIELD SUMMARY

  • State functions (path-independent): U, H, S, G, P, V, T. Heat (q) and work (w) are path functions.
  • First law: ΔU = q + w (w = work done on the system; expansion work w = −PΔV).
  • Enthalpy: ΔH < 0 exothermic. Hess's law adds reaction steps. ΔH°rxn = ΣΔH°f(products) − ΣΔH°f(reactants); ΔH°f of elements in standard state = 0. Bond enthalpies: ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed).
  • Entropy: disorder or energy dispersal; rises with gas formation, more moles of gas, dissolving, melting, higher T. Second law: ΔS_universe > 0 for spontaneous processes.
  • Gibbs: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. (−ΔH, +ΔS) always spontaneous; (+, −) never; (−, −) spontaneous at low T; (+, +) at high T.
  • Equilibrium link: ΔG° = −RT ln K. K > 1 ↔ ΔG° < 0. Q < K → forward; Q > K → reverse. At equilibrium ΔG = 0 (not ΔG°).
  • Le Châtelier: system shifts to oppose a change in concentration, pressure (toward fewer gas moles when compressed) or temperature. Only temperature changes K. Catalysts do not shift equilibrium.
  • Phase changes: temperature stays constant during a transition; heat goes to q = mL. Phase diagram: triple point, critical point; water's solid–liquid line slopes left (ice less dense).
  • Calorimetry: q = mcΔT (coffee cup, constant P → ΔH); bomb calorimeter (constant V → ΔU).
  • Kinetics: rate laws come from experiment (initial rates), not from coefficients (unless elementary). The slowest step sets the rate. Intermediates are made then consumed; catalysts are consumed then regenerated.
  • Temperature and catalysts: raising T increases the fraction of collisions above Ea (Arrhenius); catalysts lower Ea for both directions equally, so they do not change ΔG or K.

C) COMMON TRAPS + 3 MCAT-STYLE Qs

Trap 1: ΔG° vs. ΔG. ΔG° describes standard conditions (1 M, 1 atm). A reaction with positive ΔG° can still proceed if Q is small enough to make ΔG negative.

Trap 2: Writing the rate law from the balanced equation. Orders come from data or the slow elementary step. "2A + B → C" does not imply rate = k[A]²[B].

Q1. For a reaction, ΔH = +40 kJ/mol and ΔS = +100 J/(mol·K). Above what temperature is it spontaneous?

  • A) 0.4 K
  • B) 40 K
  • C) 400 K
  • D) 4,000 K

Answer: C. ΔG = 0 when T = ΔH/ΔS = 40,000 J/mol ÷ 100 J/(mol·K) = 400 K. Above that, TΔS > ΔH.

  • A is wrong: it divides 40 kJ by 100 without converting kJ to J.
  • B is wrong: it converts 40 kJ to 4,000 J instead of 40,000 J.
  • C is correct.
  • D is wrong: it converts 40 kJ to 400,000 J (one extra factor of 10).

Q2. Initial-rate data for A + B → C: doubling [A] at constant [B] quadruples the rate; doubling [B] at constant [A] has no effect. What is the rate law?

  • A) Rate = k[A][B]
  • B) Rate = k[A]²
  • C) Rate = k[A]²[B]
  • D) Rate = k[B]

Answer: B. 2ˣ = 4 → x = 2; 2ʸ = 1 → y = 0.

  • A is wrong: first order in A would only double the rate.
  • B is correct.
  • C is wrong: B is zero order.
  • D is wrong: the rate depends on A, not B.

Q3. For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH° = −92 kJ. Which change increases the equilibrium yield of NH₃ and changes K?

  • A) Raising the temperature
  • B) Lowering the temperature
  • C) Compressing the container
  • D) Adding an iron catalyst

Answer: B. For an exothermic reaction, lowering T favors products and raises K.

  • A is wrong: raising T favors the endothermic (reverse) direction and lowers K.
  • B is correct.
  • C is wrong: compression raises yield (4 gas moles → 2) but does not change K.
  • D is wrong: catalysts speed approach to equilibrium without shifting it or changing K.
